parole.significato: adenine (a base, C₅H₅N₅, found in certain glands and tissues, which pairs with thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA)
parole.testo: Ultimately borrowed from German Adenin, itself coined on the basis of Ancient Greek ἀδήν (adḗn, “gland”).

parole.significato: used to indicate various feelings: joy, excitement, fear, distress; oh! ah!
parole.testo: Borrowed from German ach (“oh”). In 16th- and 17th-century literature, o or oh was often used in this sense. In a text from 1638, German ach is translated as ok, which points to a borrowing from Russian ох (ox). The from ak, from German, was introduced in the 17th-18th century.

Borrowed from German Allergie. Coined by Austrian pediatrician Clemens von Pirquet in 1906 from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”), on the model of Energie. Featuring + -ija suffix.

parole.significato: pineapple (tropical plant with big, juicy, aromatic fruit, esp. Ananas comosus)
parole.testo: From German Ananas, from Portuguese ananás, originally from Old Tupi naná (“pineapple”).

parole.significato: apricot (tree of the family Rosaceae, especially Prunus armeniaca, with orange fruits)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Aprikose.

parole.significato: circumstance (phenomenon that exists alongside others and is connected to them)
parole.testo: Calque of German Umstand, coined by Atis Kronvalds in 1872 from ap- + the stem of the verb stāt (“to stop, to stand”) (q.v.) + -klis (cf. also apstāt (“to encircle, to surround”)). The term būšana (“being; situation”) had been previously used in this sense.

parole.significato: adverb (a word used to modify a verb, an adjective, an adverb, a phrase or a clause)
parole.testo: Literally “circumstance word,” a calque of German Umstandswort coined by Andrejs Stērste in 1879.
From German Harfe.

parole.significato: all the time; still; yet; alternative form of vēl arvien
parole.testo: Calque of German noch immer.

parole.significato: dependence (the state of that which is dependent, which is in the power, under the influence of someone, something, som…
parole.testo: Calque of German Abhängigkeit (“dependence”), coined at the end of the 19th century from atkār(t) (“to hang down”) + -ība (with atkārt from at- + kārt (“to hang”)), together with the related term atkarīgs.

parole.significato: dependent (such that it finds itself under the power, authority or influence of some person, group, nation, country, et…
parole.testo: Calque of German abhängig (“dependent”), coined at the end of the 19th century from atkār(t) (“to hang down”) + -īgs (with atkārt from at- + kārt (“to hang”)), together with the related term atkarība.

parole.significato: an Asian man, a man born in Asia or of Asian descent
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German Asiate (“Asian”).

parole.significato: glasses, eyeglasses, spectacles (sight-correcting glasses mounted on a frame)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Brille (probably from Middle Low German), ultimately from beryllium (< Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos)), the material from which the first modern glasses were made.

parole.significato: type, font (typesetting printing unit; a little metal block with a letter engraved on one side)
parole.testo: From burts (“letter”) + stabiņš (“block”) (with stabiņš from stabs (“pole, post”) + -iņš (“dim.”)). Possibly a phono-semantic matching of German Buchstabe.
Borrowed from German Zement, ultimately from Latin caementum.

parole.significato: zinc (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 30)
parole.testo: From German Zink.
German Ziffer.

parole.significato: zirconium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 40.)
parole.testo: From German Zirkonium, from Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn).

parole.significato: sugar (white, crystalline powder used to sweeten drinks and foods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zucker. First attested in the 17th century as sukurs, apparently via Livonian sukker (see sukkur). The form cukurs, with the initial s "corrected" to c [ts], occurs only later, in the 19th century.
Borrowed from German Zunft.
From daũdz + skàitlis, a calque of German Mehrzahl.

Some researchers consider this term a simple borrowing from German dumm (“stupid”). Others derive it (and its parallel o-stem dialectal variant dums) from Proto-Baltic *dum-, *dūm-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰu-, *dʰū- (“to be dusty; to whirl; to blow”), whence also dūmi (“smoke”) (q.v.). The origi
From German Dusche, from French douche.
From dzelzs (iron) + ceļš (road, way), a calque of German Eisenbahn.
Borrowed from German Dame.
Borrowed from German Herz.

parole.significato: archduke (high nobility title, above grand duke and under prince; corresponding nobleman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Erzherzog (“archduke”), itself from German Herzog (“duke”) with a prefix erz- (“arch-”).
Borrowed from German Familie, now replaced by ģimene.

parole.significato: prince (nobility title, above archduke and under king; corresponding nobleman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fürst (“Prince”).
Borrowed from German Forelle, presumably.
Apparently borrowed from German forsch (“brisk, perky, self-assertive”).
Probably from German Friseur. Compare Polish fryzjer, Danish frisør, Swedish frisör.

parole.significato: season of the year (i.e., spring, summer, autumn, winter: periods of the year characterized by different average weathe…
parole.testo: From gada (“year[gen.]”) + laiks (“time”), probably a calque of German Jahreszeit.

parole.significato: countess (nobility title, above viscountess and under marchioness; corresponding noblewoman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Graf (“count”), itself from Old High German grāfio (“ruler (of a region)”).

parole.significato: count, earl (nobility title, above viscount and under marquess; corresponding nobleman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Graf (“count”)

Possibly grāmata (“book”) + vest (“to lead”), not derived from German Buchhalter, otherwise commonly borrowed across Eastern and Central Europe, but rather a calque of German Buchführer (literally “book-leader”), which see Buchhalter for more.

parole.significato: duke (nobility title, above marquess and under grand duke; corresponding nobleman)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Herzog (“duke”).

parole.significato: education, formation (knowledge acquired by learning, usually at school)
parole.testo: Coined by Atis Kronvalds in 1869, from his earlier coinage izglītot (“to cultivate, to educate”) (from iz- + glītot (“to cultivate”), q.v.), both calques of German ausbilden (“to educate”), Ausbildung (“education, formation”). Later on (1871), Kronvalds gave preference to another coinage, dailēt, fo
Borrowed from German Kaninchen, later replaced by trusis.

Borrowed from German Karte, like kārts “playing cards” (the latter apparently having suffered the influence of kārts “pole” on its form), first attested as zemes kārte (with a long ā) in the 1850s, and later on (by the end of the 19th century) simply as karte (with a short e).
From German Kasse.
Borrowed from German Klaviatur.
From German Kleid.

parole.significato: cobalt (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 27)
parole.testo: From German Kobalt (“cobalt”).

parole.significato: suitcase, trunk (rectangular, chest-like piece of luggage for carrying clothes)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Koffer.
Borrowed from German Kreuz.
Borrowed from German Quartal.

parole.significato: diamonds (one of the four suits of playing cards, marked with the symbol ♦)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Karo, from French carreau.

parole.significato: card, playing card (one of usually 52 rectangular pieces of hard paper or cardboard with drawings, used to play various…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Karte (with level-tone lengthening: āɾ > āːɾ), itself borrowed from French carte. The term is first mentioned in 17th-century dictionaries as a plural 5th-declension noun (kārtes); the current 6th-declension form is first attested in the 1870s, perhaps as a result of the influen
Literally “time word,” a calque of German Zeitwort, coined in the 19th century by Kārlis Mīlenbahs; later replaced by P. Abuls' coinage darbības vārds.
From laiks + raksts. Calque of German Zeitschrift.
Borrowed from German Legende, from French légende, from Latin legenda.

parole.significato: noun (a word used to refer to an entity, concept or idea)
parole.testo: From lieta (“thing, object”) + vārds (“word”), a calque of German Dingwort coined by Juris Neikens in 1850 as lietu-vārds; after some variation (A. Stērste had lietas vārds in 1879, and also K. Mīlenbahs in 1895), J. Pārstrauts suggested the form lietvārds in 1881, which eventually became accepted a

parole.significato: ruler (flat, straight instrument for measuring or drawing, usually labeled with a length scale)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from German Lineal (“ruler”).

parole.significato: consonant (language sound pronounced with some kind of obstruction in the vocal tract)
parole.testo: A term coined by Atis Kronvalds in the second half of the 19th century, from līdz(i) (“(together) with”) + skan(ēt) (“to sound”), made into a 2nd-declension noun (ending -is). It is a calque of German Mitlaut, from mit (“with”) and Laut (“sound”), itself a calque of Latin cōnsonans, from cōn- (“with

parole.significato: independence (the state of one who is not subject to the control, power or authority of someone else)
parole.testo: Calque of German Unabhängigkeit (“independence”), coined at the end of the 19th century from ne- + atkarība (“dependence”) (with atkarība from atkār(t) (“to hang down”) + -ība and atkārt from at- + kārt (“to hang”)), together with the related term neatkarīgs.

parole.significato: independent, free (such that it is not subject to the control, power or authority of someone else)
parole.testo: Calque of German unabhängig, coined at the end of the 19th century from ne- + atkarīgs (“dependent”) (with atkarīgs from atkār(t) (“to hang down”) + -īgs, and atkārt from at- + kārt (“to hang”)), together with the related term neatkarība.
From German Nelke.
From German Niere.

parole.significato: a (male) Norwegian, a man from Norway
parole.testo: Apparently borrowed from German Norweger.

parole.significato: past (time period anterior to the present; circumstances previous to the present, current ones)
parole.testo: A neologism coined from pagā(jis) (“gone, passed”) + -tne by Atis Kronvalds in 1873, as a calque of German Vergangenheit (“past”), from past participle vergangen (“gone, passed”)). As a grammatical term, it was first used by A. Stērste in 1879.
Likely borrowed from German Paket, or its source, French paquet.

parole.significato: mail, post (organization that delivers letters and small packages; place, buildings where it works)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Post (itself a borrowing from Italian), first mentioned in 17th/18th-century dictionaries.

From pats (“self”) + skan(ēt) (“to sound”), made into a 2nd-declension noun (ending -is). A calque of German Selbstlaut (“vowel”) coined by Atis Kronvalds in the 1860s (initially as pašskanis). It competed with, and eventually replaced, other coinages such as G. F. Stenders' skandinieks, K. Biezbārd

parole.significato: plan, map, blueprint, layout (a detailed drawing or scheme of an object, a building, a territory)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Plan, which is itself a borrowing from French plan, from Latin planta (“sole of foot”), which is ultimately from the same stem as the adjective plāns (“thin”) below. This borrowing is first mentioned in 19th-century dictionaries.

parole.significato: medication, medicine (a pure substance or a compound of substances that is developed from natural raw materials or obta…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Präparat.

parole.significato: idea, (mental) image (subjective image, reflection of a real object or phenomenon in our conscious mind, and which can…
parole.testo: From priekš- + stāt (“to stand, to stop”), made into a 1st-declension masculine noun (ending -s). Apparently a calque of German Vorstellung.

Borrowed from German Psychose, coined in 1841 by Karl Friedrich Canstatt in his work Handbuch der Medizinischen Klinik. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “vital spirit, soul”) + -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”).
From putekļi (“dust”) + sūcējs (“sucker”), from sūkt (“to suck”). Featuring -ējs agent noun ending. Likely a calque of German Staubsauger.
From pār- (“over-”) + liecināt (“to testify, bear witness”). Possibly a calque of German überzeugen.
Borrowed from German Pik, from French pique.
Borrowed from German richtig (“correct”), replaced in the early 20th century by pareizs.
From ritenis (“wheel”) + braukšana (“riding”). Possibly a calque of German Radfahren.
Possibly borrowed from German Rosine.

parole.significato: velvet (fabric with a very dense, fine, short pile on the right side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Samt.

parole.significato: numeral (a word used to indicate a number)
parole.testo: Literally “number word,” a calque of German Zahlwort coined by Juris Neikens in 1850 as skaitļa vārdiņš; later changed by Andrejs Stērste to skaitļa vārds, which became the standard form.
From skudra (“ant”) + lācis (“bear”), a calque of German Ameisenbär.

parole.significato: statistics (mathematical science concerned with collecting, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data)
parole.testo: From German Statistik, term introduced by Gottfried Achenwall in 1748, originally referring to the analysis of data about the state, from New Latin statisticum collegium (“lecture course on state affairs”), from Italian statista (“one skilled in statecraft”), from Latin status (“state”).
From German Strauß.

parole.significato: open sandwich (a slice of bread with butter, or also with other toppings, like sausage, cheese, etc.); by extension, al…
parole.testo: From sviests (“butter”) + maize (“bread”), probably a calque from German Butterbrot; cf. also Russian бутербро́д (buterbród).
From German Takt, from French tact.

parole.significato: aunt (father's sister or mother's sister; father's brother's wife or mother's brother's wife)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Tante (“aunt”), itself a borrowing from French tante (“aunt”). This borrowing was first mentioned in 18th-century Latvian texts.
Borrowed from German Tasse or French tasse.
Borrowed from German Tastatur.

parole.significato: ink (a colored liquid used for writing)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Tinte, itself a borrowing from Latin tincta (aqua) (“colored water, liquid”). This word is first mentioned in the early 19th century. It replaced an earlier borrowing blaka, from Middle Low German blak, black (“black ink”). An attempt to introduce a neologism melne (from melns (
From German Trasse, from French trace.
Borrowed from German Tulpe.

parole.significato: blackboard, chalkboard, whiteboard (rectangular surface normally used for writing for others to read)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Tafel (“blackboard”), itself from Middle Low German tavel, tavele, from Old High German tavala, borrowed from Latin tabula (“plank, board; tablet”). The first occurrences are in 19th-century Latvian literature. (J. Endzelīns preferred the variant tāpele, since it was closer to t

parole.significato: fatherland, homeland (country or land seen as the land of one's ancestors)
parole.testo: Coined by Atis Kronvalds in 1870, in parallel with its synonym tēvija, from tēvu (“father[gen.]”) + zeme (“land”), as a calque of German Vaterland.

parole.significato: whale (large maritime mammals of the order Cetacea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Walfisch, a Germanic compound where Wal- is from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz (“whale”). The word was first borrowed (as valzivs, a compound of val- with zivs (“fish”) on the model of Wal-fisch, in the early 19th century; before that, only expressions like liela zivs “big fish” or jūr

The term vecāki (“parents”) constitutes a nominalized use of the comparative plural form of the adjective vecs (“old”) and a calque of German Eltern (“parents”). In previous centuries it was also used in the sense of “ancient ones,” “ancestors,” “elders,” “wise ones;” in the 20th century, its meanin
From viêns + skàitlis, a calque of German Einzahl.

parole.significato: tungsten (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 74.)
parole.testo: From German Wolfram.

parole.significato: all the time; uninterruptedly; still; yet
parole.testo: Apparently a calque of German immer noch (“still”).
Likely, from German Wert. Compare Lithuanian ver̃tas, Estonian väärt, Ukrainian вартість (vartistʹ).

parole.significato: soldier (especially in the czar's or in the German army)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Soldat, itself a borrowing from Italian soldato, from Vulgar Latin solidatus (“salaried (soldier)”). The word was borrowed into German in the first half of the 16th century, and into Latvian probably between the end of the 16th and the beginning of the 17th century. Its first me

Borrowed from German Socke (Baltic German söcke), from Middle Low German socke (“short socks”), from Latin soccus (“low shoe”), itself a probable borrowing from some Near East language. The first mention of this word is in a 17th-century dictionary.
Borrowing of German Silbe.

parole.significato: tartar, dental calculus (a hard, yellow deposit on the teeth)
parole.testo: From zobu (“teeth[gen.]”) + akmens (“stone”). Probably a calque of German Zahnstein.

parole.significato: soup (boiled liquid food, usually containing meat, fish, vegetables or cereal products)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Suppe, itself partly via French soupe, partly via Middle Low German sope, from Proto-Germanic *supô (compare also sūpen “to drink; to eat with a spoon,” German saufen “to drink; to booze”), ultimately from the same Proto-Indo-European stem (*seu-, *sū- “juice; moisture”) as the

parole.significato: a (male) Swede, a man from Sweden
parole.testo: Apparently borrowed from German Schwede (“Swede”), though the form is somewhat anomalous (extra r, initial z instead of š).
Borrowed from German Saal. Compare Lithuanian salė.
Borrowed from German Gift (“poison”), now replaced by the 20th-century coinage inde.
Borrowed from German Körper (“body”), replaced at the end of the 19th century by ķermenis.

Borrowed from German Kürbis, itself borrowed from Latin cucurbita (from an earlier *curbitia, via reduplication). This word is first mentioned in early 18th-century texts, but only in the 19th century did it become really popular and enter the standard literary language. Various expressions had prev
Borrowed from German Schlips (“necktie”).
Borrowed from German schwach (“weak”). Compare Dutch zwak, Swedish svag.

parole.significato: spirit (distilled beverage), liquor (especially vodka or schnapps)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Schnaps.
